title: Weak point Wednesday: forearms
summary: He rejects the idea that forearms are purely genetic, explains how insertions and wrist size affect apparent forearm size, and shares his own stats (13-13.5 in forearms, 6.5 in wrists, goal 15 in). His approach: use straps and train forearms directly with finger curls, supported wrist curls, behind-the-back wrist curls and reverse curls on arm days, plus isometric grip work (cone grips, towel) and banded pre-pumped dead hangs, arguing that loaded stretch rather than gripping itself drives growth.

claims.claim: Forearms aren't purely genetic: good genetics make some body parts easier, but no body part refuses to grow.
Forearm genetics mostly refers to insertions; a longer muscle has more size potential.
Forearm size is partly illusion: a large wrist competes with the forearm and makes it look blocky, while bodybuilding aesthetics rely on round curvature, like a quad sweep.
Pro bodybuilders inject synthol and site-enhancement oil to make muscles look round and pop.
His brachioradialis is well developed from years of gripper work and his inner forearm from lots of curls, but the front/top of his forearm lags.
His forearms measure 13-13.5 inches and his wrists 6.5 inches, well below the roughly 7.2-inch US average he cites, so his forearms look bigger than they measure; he aims for 15 inches.
Using straps doesn't hurt forearm development; holding the bar is just an isometric hold, which is useful but not everything.
Forearms need wrist flexion, elbow flexion and every angle; pulls and rows alone won't build them unless you're genetically gifted, so do dedicated isolation work.
Regular wrist curls hurt his wrists; the only version that works for him is with the forearm resting on the leg using fixed dumbbells, because plates on adjustable dumbbells rotate around the handle.
On arm days he does standing behind-the-back wrist curls, finger curls and reverse curls as forearm isolation, plus lots of isometric pulls and holds.
He uses accessory grip holds like cone grips (lifting the bar from the side with a forearm twist and squeezing) and towel holds, for about 15 seconds.
Dead hangs are good for forearms; he pre-pumps with a band, does the hang, then pumps again afterwards.
What grows forearms in deadlifts, pull-ups and rows is weighted stretch, not the act of gripping; squeezing air hard does nothing, but holding something that pulls on the muscle causes hypertrophy.
Forearms are the one body part fully visible in jeans and a shirt, so developing them is critical.

exercises.name: Seated wrist curl (forearm on leg, fixed dumbbell)
cues: rest arm and weight on the leg
use fixed dumbbells, not plate-loaded ones that rotate
exercises.why: the only wrist curl variation that doesn't hurt his wrists

exercises.name: Cone grip
cues: lift the bar from the side with a twist of the forearm
squeeze as hard as possible ~15 s

exercises.name: Dead hang with band pre-pump
cues: pre-pump the forearm with a band
